title: Slash the Guitarist Now Has a Snake Named After Him
summary:
A rock legend just got one of the strangest honors in science: a snake named after him.

Researchers have identified a new species from the tropical forests of New Guinea and named it Lielaphis slashi — "Slash's groundsnake." Slash, whose real name is Saul Hudson, is the guitarist for Guns N' Roses. But he's also been fascinated by reptiles for most of his life and has long supported zoos and natural history museums. "As a long time herpephile, I am extremely honored and humbled," Slash said. (A herpephile is someone who loves reptiles.)

For Sara Ruane, the Field Museum's Associate Curator of Herpetology, the name is personal. She's loved Guns N' Roses since first grade, and by fifth grade she had already told her teacher she wanted to be a herpetologist — a scientist who studies reptiles. At twelve, she saw a magazine cover of Slash holding his pet reticulated python. "This guy is so cool," she remembers thinking.

The snake itself is reddish-brown and about 28 inches long. It was collected in New Guinea, the world's second-largest island, whose tropical forests hold enormous biodiversity — much of it still undocumented. Chris Austin, a professor at Louisiana State University, first spotted the snake during nighttime fieldwork in 2006. These groundsnakes are nocturnal, hunting just after sunset at the base of large trees. "When working at night in New Guinea you need to be very careful as there are several highly venomous species that look very similar," Austin warned.

At first the snake didn't obviously look new. But genetic analyses showed it was distinct from similar snakes in the same genus. Differences in scale counts and ecological modeling of its preferred habitat confirmed it. "The combination of physical characteristics... and the genetic evidence is what led us to realize that it is an entirely new species," said Tianqi Huang, the study's first author.

Scientists still know little about how it lives. Its large back teeth suggest it grabs slippery lizards and reptile eggs rather than squeezing prey like a boa constrictor.

A guitarist, a childhood dream, and a brand-new snake — science can be surprisingly cool.
why_it_matters: Most of Earth's species are still unknown, and the work of finding and naming them depends on public support and on young people choosing careers in field biology — so a story that links a guitar hero to a new snake can quietly recruit the next generation of scientists.

background_read: Slash (the guitarist of the rock band Guns N' Roses, whose real name is Saul Hudson) is the latest celebrity to have an animal named after him, a tradition scientists use to draw attention to new discoveries. In the past, researchers have named a horse fly after the singer Beyoncé and a spider after the musician Neil Young.

The snake comes from New Guinea (the world's second-largest island, north of Australia and shared between Indonesia and Papua New Guinea), whose rainforests are among the most species-rich places on Earth but are still poorly surveyed.

The people behind the study work at institutions such as the Field Museum (a natural history museum in Chicago) and Louisiana State University, and they are trained in taxonomy — the science of classifying living things, where every new species must be formally described and published under international rules.
Because many tropical species are discovered in forests that are being logged, some animals may already be losing their habitat before scientists have learned much about them.

perspectives.description: Naming a snake after Slash brings rare publicity to a small, underfunded field, and it also honours Slash's own decades of support for zoos and natural history museums. Fans who would never read a taxonomy paper may now know that a species called Lielaphis slashi exists.

Some researchers worry that celebrity names turn careful science into a publicity stunt and overshadow the people who did the hard fieldwork in the forest. There is also a conservation worry: the snake's rainforest habitat is under pressure from logging, and a famous name does not automatically protect the land.

Naming species after famous people is an old habit used to attract attention and funding, and the real scientific weight here sits in the genetics and the scale counts that proved this was a new species rather than a look-alike. The name is the headline; the evidence is the science.

Because so much of New Guinea's wildlife is still undocumented, the open question is whether the attention converts into money for surveys and habitat protection. It also raises a personal question: will Sara Ruane's story — a childhood dream that became a career — encourage other kids to become herpetologists?
